abstract.t: This document specifies the Secure Transport Communication Protocol (STCP). Its intended status is Standards Track. This initial draft records verified implementation behavior and identifies remaining interoperability and security specification work.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: STCP is a transport protocol with compact framing, X25519 key establishment, and AES-256-GCM-protected data and control messages. The wire version is distinct from the product version.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 ( and ) when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This initial draft also records implementation observations and explicitly identified open design questions. Descriptions of current Linux behavior are not automatically normative requirements for independent implementations.

section.name: Architecture and Transport Mapping
section.t: STCP uses standards-compliant TCP and UDP as underlying transports. The TCP and UDP protocols are outside the scope of this specification.

section.name: Linux Socket API Mapping (Implementation-Specific)
section.t: The reviewed Linux kernel module defines AF_STCP and PF_STCP as 45. The protocol argument to socket() selects the STCP carrier: STCP_PROTO_DEFAULT (0) and STCP_PROTO_TCP (253) select TCP, while STCP_PROTO_UDP (254) selects UDP. These constants are Linux implementation API selectors; they are not assigned IP Protocol or IPv6 Next Header values and do not appear in the outer IP header as STCP protocol numbers. The implementation registers a struct proto with proto_register(), a struct net_proto_family with sock_register(), and its own struct proto_ops including bind, connect, listen, accept, sendmsg, recvmsg, poll, shutdown, and socket-option callbacks. This section describes the implementation and does not require other operating systems to adopt Linux numeric constants or APIs.

section.name: Scope and Deployment Considerations
section.t: Congestion control for STCP traffic over UDP remains an open specification and verification requirement (see ).

The base STCP handshake intentionally does not authenticate peer identity. Active attackers can substitute handshake public keys and perform a man-in-the-middle attack. Implementations and deployments MUST NOT interpret successful key establishment or AES-GCM verification alone as proof of peer identity. Fatal protocol or cryptographic failures are distinct from ordinary carrier packet loss, which may be handled by the specified reliability procedures.

section.name: Wire Format
section.t: Each frame starts with a 17-octet header. Octet 0 is the descriptor: bits 0-3 packet type, bits 4-5 wire version (3), and bits 6-7 flags. Octets 1-4 contain the payload length; octets 5-8 the sequence; octets 9-12 the acknowledgment; and octets 13-16 the connection ID. All multioctet integers are big-endian.

Packet types are PublicKey (1), HandshakeDone (2), DataChunk (3), DataChunkEnd (4), Ack (5), Ping (6), Pong (7), Close (8), and Reset (9). PublicKey has a 32-octet payload; HandshakeDone has no payload. The implementation rejects unknown versions and packet types.

section.name: Framing over TCP and UDP
section.t: STCP uses the same 17-octet header and length-delimited frame encoding over both supported carriers. The payload length at header offsets 1 through 4 is an unsigned 32-bit integer in network byte order and counts the octets following the header. The complete frame length is therefore 17 plus the encoded payload length. A receiver MUST validate the descriptor, frame type, and applicable length bounds before consuming the complete frame.

section.name: TCP Byte-Stream Mapping
section.t: TCP carries an ordered byte stream without application message boundaries. An STCP frame is serialized as its 17-octet header immediately followed by the number of payload octets indicated by that header; successive frames are concatenated without a separate carrier-level delimiter or length prefix. A TCP read can contain a partial header, a partial payload, one frame, or portions of multiple frames. The STCP receiver buffers incomplete data and MUST NOT interpret a frame until its complete header and payload have arrived. The current Linux implementation uses a bounded receive queue, peeks at the header when 17 octets are available, and waits until the complete frame length is buffered. Its TCP carrier loops over partial kernel_sendmsg() results until all submitted bytes have been sent or a terminal error occurs.

section.name: UDP Datagram Mapping
section.t: UDP carries datagrams rather than a reliable ordered stream. The current Linux UDP carrier passes each received datagram and its peer IPv4 address and UDP port to the STCP Rust receive path. The listener uses the STCP connection ID in the first complete header to find or create a per-peer session; a new session is admitted only from a PublicKey frame with a complete 32-octet key payload, and packets from an unexpected source address or port for an existing session are discarded. UDP transmission uses kernel_sendmsg() for a datagram and treats a partial send as an error. The precise requirements for one versus multiple STCP frames per UDP datagram, datagram truncation, and malformed trailing bytes remain to be made normative after verification across all implementations; this draft does not yet assert a one-frame-per-datagram rule.

section.name: Implementation Frame Bounds
section.t: The reviewed Rust implementation defines a 60-KiB UDP DATA payload target and a 2-MiB stream DATA payload target, with an 8-octet transmitted nonce and 16-octet authentication tag. The decoder also applies packet-type-specific payload bounds: PublicKey is exactly 32 octets, HandshakeDone is empty, and the header decoder caps protected control payloads at 24 octets. The protected control payload format requires exactly 24 octets (see ). These values describe implementation behavior; negotiated and interoperable maximum-frame-size requirements remain open.

section.name: Handshake and State Transitions
section.t: The implementation states are New, Bound, Listening, Handshake, Ready, Closed, and Error. The handshake procedures described below are observed in the 2026-11-02 Linux source snapshot; complete wire-level error semantics are not yet standardized.

li.t: When a connection enters Handshake with an attached carrier, the local endpoint sends a PublicKey frame. Its 32-octet payload contains the local X25519 public key. The PublicKey frame advertises the COMPRESSION_CAPABLE flag.

On receiving a PublicKey frame, the implementation requires a 32-octet payload and rejects flags other than COMPRESSION_CAPABLE. It derives directional traffic keys from the peer public key and sends an empty HandshakeDone frame.

The receiver permits HandshakeDone to arrive before PublicKey and remembers its receipt. The handshake parser stops before consuming subsequent application DATA when the required handshake inputs are present.

The local connection transitions to Ready only when local traffic keys have been derived and a peer HandshakeDone has been received. An established application DATA frame must not be interpreted as a handshake frame.

section.t: PublicKey and HandshakeDone are not protected by the established-session DATA or control authentication mechanism. In particular, HandshakeDone does not prove the peer's identity or cryptographically bind the full handshake transcript. The base protocol does not authenticate peer identity.

section.name: Handshake Wire Requirements
section.t: A PublicKey frame carries exactly 32 octets of X25519 public-key material. A receiver MUST reject a PublicKey frame with any other payload length. A HandshakeDone frame carries no payload; a receiver MUST reject a nonempty HandshakeDone frame. The only permitted PublicKey flag in the reviewed implementations is COMPRESSION_CAPABLE. A receiver MUST NOT interpret an unknown flag as a negotiated capability.

An endpoint MUST NOT enter the established application-data state until it has derived directional traffic keys from the peer PublicKey and received the peer HandshakeDone. An endpoint MUST NOT send DATA before entering that state. A receiver MUST allow HandshakeDone to precede PublicKey and retain that event for the establishment decision. When both handshake inputs have been processed, a receiver MUST leave subsequent complete DATA frames for established-session processing rather than consuming them as unexpected handshake frames. Over TCP, an endpoint MUST buffer partial headers and payloads until a complete frame is available.

In the reviewed Linux implementation, a complete DATA frame encountered by the handshake parser while either handshake input is missing produces a protocol error. Repeated empty HandshakeDone frames encountered in that parser set the same receipt flag. If multiple valid PublicKey frames are consumed in one parser pass before both handshake inputs are available, the last one consumed is used for key derivation. These observations describe the implementation and do not define duplicate-key handling for interoperability.

These requirements do not mandate a particular internal state enumeration or parser-loop implementation. Wire-visible responses to duplicate handshake frames, invalid flags, unsupported versions, timeouts, and premature DATA remain open. If a handshake failure makes key establishment impossible, or if a local protocol or cryptographic state failure makes continued processing unsafe, the endpoint MUST terminate the connection, stop using its traffic keys, and stop accepting new application DATA on that connection. An endpoint MUST NOT deliver DATA that has failed authentication. Discarding a replayed control frame according to and recovering from ordinary packet loss according to are normal receive and recovery procedures.

section.name: Directional Key Derivation
section.t: Endpoints MUST derive the directional DATA keys from the 32-octet X25519 shared secret and the two 32-octet public keys. The salt input orders the public keys by role, with the client public key first, regardless of frame arrival order. The derivation is:

li.t: client_to_server_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM client to server key") || 0x01).
server_to_client_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM server to client key") || 0x01).

section.t: The operator || denotes byte concatenation. Endpoints MUST encode the labels exactly as shown in ASCII, without a terminating NUL. The suffix 0x01 is a single octet. The client MUST use the client-to-server DATA key for transmission and the server-to-client DATA key for reception. The server MUST use the reverse assignment. If the two directional DATA keys are equal, the endpoint MUST terminate the connection. Derive each directional control key as specified in .
The literal STCPv4 prefix is part of the DATA key derivation labels for wire version 3.

section.name: Packet Protection
section.t: DataChunk and DataChunkEnd frames MUST use AES-256-GCM with the directional DATA key. The payload consists of an 8-octet unsigned nonce in network byte order, the ciphertext, and a 16-octet authentication tag. The payload length in the header includes all three fields.

Ack, Ping, Pong, Close, and Reset frames MUST use the directional control key. Their payload is exactly 24 octets: the 8-octet nonce followed by a 16-octet authentication tag generated over empty plaintext. For each direction, the control key is the 32-octet HMAC-SHA-256 output keyed by that direction's DATA key. The HMAC input is the ASCII string STCP wire3 control AES256-GCM key followed by a single octet of value 0x01.

For both DATA and protected control frames, the additional authenticated data (AAD) MUST be all 17 octets of the encoded wire header in wire order. The 12-octet GCM IV MUST consist of four zero octets followed by the eight transmitted nonce octets in wire order.

section.name: Nonce and Replay Handling
section.t: Each direction MUST use independent DATA and control nonce counters, each starting at zero for its corresponding fresh key. A sender MUST NOT wrap a counter or use the same nonce for a new encryption under the same key. If a fresh nonce is unavailable under the current key, the sender MUST terminate the connection. A reliable DATA retransmission MUST resend the original encoded frame byte for byte.

The receiver MUST verify the authentication tag before delivering DATA or acting on a protected control frame. For each receive control key, the receiver MUST maintain a 64-position sliding replay window. It MUST discard duplicate nonces and values at least 64 below the greatest accepted nonce. A frame that fails authentication MUST NOT advance the replay window. In-order DATA delivery checks the expected sequence and nonce after authentication. Authenticated out-of-order DATA can be buffered.

section.name: Reliability, Acknowledgments and Retransmission
section.t: The following values describe the reviewed Linux implementation rather than negotiated protocol parameters. Reliability is enabled when the carrier reports that STCP reliability is required; the TCP carrier does not run the STCP retransmission timer.

section.name: Send Window and Segmentation
section.t: The implementation uses a fixed maximum of eight outstanding reliable DATA frames per connection. An application send that would exceed the pending-frame limit returns a retry indication instead of adding the frames. Application data is split into DataChunk frames, with DataChunkEnd marking the last frame of a send. This limit is a frame-count bound, not a receiver-advertised congestion window.

section.name: Cumulative ACK Processing
section.t: ACK values are cumulative. On receipt of a valid authenticated ACK with acknowledgment number A, the sender removes pending frames whose sequence numbers are less than or equal to A. An ACK referring to a sequence not yet transmitted is treated as a protocol error. The receiver normally sends an ACK after four received frames; selected events can force an earlier ACK. Duplicate-ACK recovery can resend the latest cumulative acknowledgment. When acknowledged frames release pending capacity, blocked senders are awakened.

section.name: Round-Trip Time Estimation
section.t: The initial retransmission timeout (RTO) is 60 milliseconds. The timer tick is 20 milliseconds, and the RTO is clamped between 20 and 3000 milliseconds. An RTT sample is collected only from a frame that has not been retransmitted, avoiding ambiguous samples as in Karn's algorithm. On the first sample R, SRTT is R and RTTVAR is max(1, floor(R/2)). On subsequent samples, RTTVAR becomes floor((3*RTTVAR + abs(SRTT-R))/4) and SRTT becomes floor((7*SRTT + R)/8). RTO becomes clamp(SRTT + 4*RTTVAR, 20, 3000) milliseconds. These integer formulas reflect the current implementation.

section.name: Retransmission Timer
section.t: For each pending frame, the implementation maintains an age in timer ticks, a per-frame RTO and a retry count. On expiry it resends the stored encrypted frame bytes without generating a new nonce. Per-frame RTO doubles after a retransmission, capped at 3000 milliseconds. No more than four pending frames are selected for retransmission per timer tick. After eight retries for a pending frame, the connection reports a terminal timeout corresponding to ETIMEDOUT. The implementation updates retransmission and timeout counters.

section.name: STCP Congestion Control over UDP
section.t: STCP currently limits the number of outstanding frames and retransmissions per timer tick. A congestion response for STCP traffic over UDP remains to be specified and validated before deployment over arbitrary Internet paths.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Because the base handshake lacks peer identity authentication, an active man-in-the-middle can substitute public keys. AES-GCM protection after key establishment does not prevent this attack. Nonce uniqueness, session-key freshness, reconnect behavior, and cross-platform interoperability require further verification. The connection ID is not an authentication credential.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This initial version requests no allocation. The Linux STCP_PROTO_TCP value 253 and STCP_PROTO_UDP value 254 are local AF_STCP socket API selectors, not allocations in the IP Protocol Numbers registry. IP protocol number 253 is reserved for experimentation and is not a permanent STCP assignment. Direct STCP carriage over IP is not currently implemented and is outside the scope of this draft. No permanent IP protocol number is requested. Any future native-IP specification and allocation request require separate work.

section.name: Outstanding Work
section.t: Before Standards Track publication, the draft needs complete normative state-machine and error rules, cross-platform verification of the KDF test vectors, carrier mapping, compression negotiation, UDP congestion control, security review, and interoperability evidence. This document does not claim IETF approval.
